subject: Service degradation scenarios, priority routing and recovery SLAs (RTO/RPO)
messages:
From: Diane Chu <diane.chu@crestlane.com>

Cc: Elliot Ramos <elliot.ramos@crestlane.com>, Procurement <procurement@crestlane.com>

Subject: Clarification on partial-region degradation, RTO/RPO and request for routing controls

Alex —

Thanks again for the quick demo last week. As we compile answers for the Crestlane RFP I have a few follow-ups specific to partial-region degradation and our multi-region resiliency requirements. We're trying to map gap items and acceptable mitigations. Can you confirm the following points in writing so I can share with our infrastructure & procurement teams?

1) If an availability zone or a subset of GPUs in a region degrade (not full-region outage), what automatic actions does Redwood take vs. what requires manual operator intervention?
2) What are typical RTO/RPO figures we can claim for: (a) full-region evacuation to another region, (b) degraded-node recovery where some requests are served with increased latency, and (c) persistence-layer recovery for customer-managed VPC/private deployments?
3) Can requests be prioritized by customer or route so that high-priority transactions are routed to warm capacity while bulk/non-critical requests are throttled? How do you guarantee isolation across customers under heavy degradation?
4) For stateful/cached workloads (prefix / KV cache), what is the expected cache warm-up time after failover and what mitigations exist to reduce inference-quality regression?

Attached is the Crestlane DR questionnaire — I've flagged the relevant sections. Appreciate anything concise we can include in our submission.

Best,
Diane
Diane Chu
Senior Cloud Architect — Crestlane Financial

From: Alex Martinez <alex.martinez@redwood.com>
To: Diane Chu <diane.chu@crestlane.com>
Cc: marissa.cole@redwood.com, ben.carter@redwood.com
Date: Tue, 7 Sep 2026 10:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Clarification on partial-region degradation, RTO/RPO and request for routing controls

Diane —

Thanks for the clear list. Below are concise, exportable answers you can drop into the RFP. I've included a short note on operational playbooks and a link to a sample evidence pack; attaching the formal PDF and the evidence bundle as well. If you want, Ben can run a short tabletop to walk through the sequence with your infra team.

Summary answers (concise):

1) Partial-region degradation handling:
- Automatic: health-aware request routing removes degraded hosts from the pool, continuous batching redistributes inflight work, and smart routing shifts traffic to healthy AZs/regions based on policy. These actions are automated and typically complete within policy windows (see RTO below).
- Manual: operator-initiated capacity reallocation (e.g., spinning additional dedicated nodes, changing quantization profile for emergency throughput) is manual and typically needed only for prolonged capacity shortages or hardware replacement.

2) RTO / RPO (typical figures we provide for contractual language):
- Full-region evacuation (automatic routing to another region): RTO goal = 10–20 minutes to re-route traffic and warm cross-region caches; RPO = best-effort for in-flight token state; stateless inference results preserved, persistent job checkpoints (if applicable) rely on customer persistence settings.
- Degraded-node recovery (partial slowdown): RTO goal = 2–10 minutes for affected nodes to be drained and traffic redistributed; observed latency increases are mitigated by degraded-path routing and autoscaling where available.
- Customer-managed VPC / Private deployment persistence: RTO = 30–120 minutes depending on on-prem resource provisioning and network reconfiguration; RPO = configured via customer replication (we recommend cross-site replication for critical KV/state).

3) Priority routing and isolation:
- Yes. Redwood supports per-customer and per-route priority tiers. Priority routing can be enforced by policy: route pins (high priority) route to reserved/warm pools, while lower-priority traffic uses burstable/shared capacity. Throttles and rejection policies can be applied at the API gateway level to prevent noisy neighbor effects. Dedicated capacity contracts guarantee isolation for committed pools.

4) Cache/KV warm-up and mitigation:
- Expected cold-warm window: 1–30 minutes depending on cache size and query distribution.
- Mitigations: prefix caching for repeated prompts, pre-warming using replayable prompt sets during failover, and model-variant fallbacks (smaller quantized model) to maintain throughput while regenerating higher-quality cached responses.

Operational notes:
- We document a runbook for DR rehearsals and can provide a runbook extract showing exact steps (routing changes, cache rehydration, escalation contacts).
- For enterprise customers we offer scheduled regional-recovery rehearsals and an evidence pack including trunk-level logs and trace spans for one rehearsal event.

I've attached crestlane-dr-qa-answers.pdf and an evidence bundle. Let me know if you want an explicit contractual RTO line to include (we can propose a 15-minute re-route SLA for Dedicated customers with a corresponding credit schedule).

Thanks,
Alex Martinez
Enterprise Sales Engineer | Redwood Inference

Alex — quick double-check before we send final PDF to Crestlane procurement: can we tighten the RTO language for the Dedicated offering into a single line? Procurement always wants crisp commitments. Suggestion: "For Dedicated capacity customers, Redwood will re-route traffic to an alternate region within 15 minutes under automated failover conditions; this is the contractual RTO for region-level evacuations."

Ben — please confirm this is safe from an SRE/ops perspective and whether we want to add the caveat about scheduled maintenance windows.

Marissa
Director, Strategic Accounts

Marissa / Alex —
All good with Marissa's suggested contract language for Dedicated customers. Operational caveats to include:
- Excludes large-scale cloud-provider region outages that require cross-cloud coordination; documented exceptions in the SLA.
- Credit/penalty schedule tied to incident classification and customer observability (we require tracing to confirm routing cutover time).
- For private/VPC deployments, the 15-minute commitment only applies when customer has pre-allocated warm standby nodes and network peering is preconfigured; otherwise default RTOs apply.

I'll add a one-page appendix to the PDF called "Operational caveats & evidence required" before we publish.

Ben
Principal Solutions Architect
